conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the vascular surgeons. You’re here today for a planned procedure on your transplanted kidney, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. They told me it’s called a coil embolization. I’m a bit nervous—what exactly does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s a minimally invasive procedure where we block the blood flow to your failed transplant kidney using small metal coils. This helps avoid a major surgery to remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it’s not being taken out? I thought they might have to cut it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Because of your prior abdominal surgeries and mesh repair, removing it surgically could be risky. This is a safer option to let the kidney shrink over time without infection or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Will I feel anything during the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be given sedation, so you’ll be very relaxed and won’t feel pain. We’ll go through a small puncture in your groin to reach the artery. It usually takes about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better than open surgery. What about after? Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to stay flat in bed for a few hours to prevent bleeding at the site. Then, if all goes well, you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I do have a lot of medical history—kidney transplant, heart issues, thyroid—will that affect anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history. Your atrial fibrillation and thyroid condition are stable. We’ll continue your usual meds, except for a few adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant team recommended stopping Myfortic and starting a short course of steroids to help with inflammation. You’ll also keep taking tacrolimus as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve been on Myfortic for years. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because the transplant kidney isn’t working anymore, we don’t need strong immunosuppression. The steroid taper will help your body adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my warfarin? I’ve been off it since my last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart it soon—your team plans for you to take 4 mg on Thursday, then follow up with your nephrologist for dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I was worried about my stroke risk with atrial fib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re balancing bleeding and clotting risks carefully. Now, let’s get you prepped for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well yesterday with the coil embolization. No complications, and the site looks clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I felt a little pressure but no pain. How long do I need to stay in bed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve already completed the 4-hour bed rest. You can sit up and walk now. We’ll monitor your blood pressure and the groin site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I walked a little earlier—felt fine. But my blood pressure drops after dialysis. I take midodrine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nephrology reviewed that. They’ll contact your nephrologist to adjust your midodrine if needed. For now, keep taking it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I just get anxious when my BP drops too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll keep an eye on it. You also had dialysis yesterday as scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in the afternoon. I felt a bit weak afterward, but better by evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. Your labs this morning are stable—creatinine is 4.4, which is expected since you’re on dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood count? I’ve been anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hemoglobin is 9.6, a bit low but stable. No signs of bleeding. We’ll monitor it at your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re preparing your discharge orders. You’re doing well—eating, walking, no pain or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, except Myfortic is stopped. You’ll take prednisone for six days—40 mg for three days, then 20 mg for three—then stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, short course. And tacrolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three 0.5 mg capsules every 12 hours. Keep taking your other meds: amiodarone, levothyroxine, pravastatin, and valganciclovir twice a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 4 mg on Thursday. Your INR will be checked soon after. Don’t miss that follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. What about the incision? I don’t even have a big cut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a small puncture. Keep it clean and dry. You can shower, but no baths or swimming until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acetaminophen for mild pain. Oxycodone if needed, but don’t drive while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When should I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever over 101.5, severe pain, redness at the site, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Also, if you vomit and can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ll follow up with my nephrologist and transplant team?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll monitor your kidney function, INR, and adjust meds as needed. You’re doing well—this was a success.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel relieved this is done without major surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll discharge you in a couple of hours. Keep walking daily, no heavy lifting until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge papers are ready. You can go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. See you at your follow-up.
